cards.front: Recall a key point about Gender Representation
cards.back: Gender representation has been a central concern of media studies because media products both reflect and shape cultural attitudes about masculinity and femininity.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Gender Representation
cards.back: Laura Mulvey's 'male gaze' (1975): mainstream cinema positions audiences to view women through a heterosexual male perspective, objectifying their bodies for visual pleasure.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Gender Representation
cards.back: Traditional female stereotypes: damsel in distress, sex object, nagging wife, career woman (as threat), mother/housewife, femme fatale. These reduce complex identities to simple traits.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Gender Representation
cards.back: Traditional male stereotypes: action hero, family man, buffoon (in sitcoms), businessman, villain, lad. Masculinity is often linked to physical strength, stoicism, and control.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Gender Representation
cards.back: The Bechdel Test: a film passes if it has two named female characters who talk to each other about something other than a man. Many mainstream films still fail this basic test.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Gender Representation
cards.back: Changing representations: contemporary media increasingly features complex, non-stereotypical female characters — e.g. strong female protagonists, women in leadership roles, and diverse body types.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Gender Representation
cards.back: The 'new man': a representation of men as emotionally expressive, nurturing, and domestically competent — a contrast to traditional hyper-masculinity. Advertising has adopted this representation.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Gender Representation
cards.back: Toxic masculinity: media representations that equate masculinity with aggression, emotional suppression, and dominance can reinforce harmful gender expectations for men.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Gender Representation
cards.back: LGBTQ+ representation: historically marginalised, stereotyped (the 'sissy', the 'predatory lesbian'), or invisible. Recent progress includes more diverse and central LGBTQ+ characters.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Gender Representation
cards.back: Intersectionality: gender representation intersects with race, class, age, sexuality, and disability. White, middle-class women are better represented than women of colour, working-class women, or disabled women.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Gender Representation
cards.back: Representation is improving but uneven — some media forms (streaming, indie games) are more progressive, while others (blockbuster films, music videos) remain stereotypical.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Gender Representation
cards.back: Audience response matters: social media enables audiences to critique and challenge poor representations, creating pressure on producers to improve (e.g. #OscarsSoWhite).

cards.front: What should you know about media studies exam tips — gender representation?
cards.back: 1. For Gender Representation, use media terminology precisely (e.g. connotation, denotation, representation, ideology) 2. Always analyse how media language creates meaning for specific audiences 3. Reference specific examples from set products to support your analysis 4. When evaluating Gender Representation, consider the role of media industries and cultural contexts 5. For extended answers, debate different interpretations before reaching your own
Evaluate the view that media representations of gender are becoming more progressive. Refer to your CSPs. [15 marks]
